summary: This document specifies an IP-based encapsulation for MPLS called MPLS-in-UDP, for situations where UDP encapsulation is preferred to direct use of MPLS, such as to enable UDP-based ECMP or link aggregation.

plainLanguage.summary: MPLS packets can be put inside ordinary UDP packets, like a letter in a regular envelope, so networks that don't understand MPLS can still carry them.

subtitle: Carry MPLS packets inside UDP so ordinary IP routers can spread them across multiple paths.

tldr.problem: Existing IP encapsulations for MPLS spread traffic over parallel paths using IP addresses or special header fields, and IPv4 has no entropy field. Routers already hash UDP ports for load balancing.
tldr.mechanism: MPLS-in-UDP puts the MPLS label stack and message body after a UDP header whose source port carries entropy and whose destination port is 6635.
tldr.outcome: It is for a single network, or closely cooperating networks, that manage congestion. It MUST NOT be used over the general Internet to carry traffic that is not congestion controlled.

today: RFC 7510 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2015. The unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Put MPLS in UDP
sections.content:
Several IP-based encapsulations for MPLS already exist, such as MPLS-in-IP, MPLS-in-GRE (RFC 4023) and MPLS-in-L2TPv3 (RFC 4817). They let two Label Switching Routers be adjacent on a Label Switched Path while separated by an IP network. Load balancing with them relies on varying IP addresses or on protocol fields such as the GRE Key or the L2TPv3 Session ID. IPv6 can use its Flow Label, but IPv4 has no such entropy field.

Most existing routers already distribute traffic over Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP) paths and Link Aggregation Groups (LAGs) using a hash of the five-tuple of UDP and TCP packets: source address, destination address, source port, destination port and protocol. Using the UDP source port as an entropy field lets that existing capability balance MPLS traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Many network machines already know how to share UDP traffic across several roads by looking at its port numbers. Wrapping MPLS in UDP lets them do the same for MPLS.

sections.title: Where It May Be Used
sections.content:
MPLS-in-UDP MUST only be deployed within a single network with a single operator, or within networks of an adjacent set of cooperating operators, where traffic is managed to avoid congestion. It is not for the Internet, where congestion control is required. Packet filters SHOULD be added to stop MPLS-in-UDP packets from escaping the network because of misconfiguration or packet errors.

The document defines only the data-plane encapsulation. How a router learns that the far end can decapsulate MPLS-in-UDP, by manual configuration or by dynamic advertisement, is outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: This trick is meant for private road networks run by one owner or by close friends who agree on the rules, not for the public highway.

sections.title: The Encapsulation Format
sections.content:
The packet is a UDP header followed by an MPLS label stack (RFC 3032) and one MPLS message body.

  • Source port: a 16-bit entropy value chosen by the encapsulator to identify a flow. How a flow is defined and how the value is computed is left to the encapsulator. If no entropy is needed, all packets of a flow SHOULD use the same randomly selected constant, to avoid reordering. To keep the port within 49152 to 65535, the encapsulator SHOULD compute a 14-bit hash and set the two top bits to binary 11.
  • Destination port: 6635, allocated by IANA to mean the payload is an MPLS packet.
  • UDP length: as in RFC 768.
  • UDP checksum: for IPv4 it is RECOMMENDED to be zero, for performance or implementation reasons, unless checksum protection of VPN labels matters. For IPv6 it MUST be a real checksum, unless one of the exceptions below applies.
sections.plainLanguage: The outer envelope has a return address that is really just a random-looking number to help sorting, and a fixed delivery address meaning 'this holds MPLS'.

sections.title: Processing Procedures
sections.content:
The encapsulator fills the source port with its entropy value and the destination port with 6635. Whether the top label is downstream-assigned or upstream-assigned follows RFC 5332. If the tunnel destination address is unicast, the top label MUST be downstream-assigned. If it is multicast, all packets in that tunnel use one kind or the other, and without other knowledge the label SHOULD be presumed upstream-assigned.

Intermediate routers may balance the packets using the hash of the UDP five-tuple. The decapsulator removes the UDP header and processes the MPLS packet. For MTU and fragmentation, TTL and differentiated services, the Common Procedures of RFC 4023 SHOULD be followed.

Each UDP tunnel is unidirectional: traffic goes to the allocated destination port and is never sent back to a source port, which only provides entropy. Middleboxes such as firewalls often assume a shared port pair for two-way traffic, so passing bidirectional MPLS-in-UDP through them may need separate configuration per direction.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender stamps the envelope, the sorting machines share the envelopes among lanes, and the receiver opens the envelope. The envelopes only travel one way.

sections.title: The IPv6 Zero-Checksum Rules
sections.content:
Over IPv6 the UDP checksum protects the IPv6 and UDP headers, so it MUST be used unless the requirements of RFC 6935 and RFC 6936 for UDP zero-checksum mode are met. Three exceptions allow zero-checksum mode: a single-administration network where corruption is known to be exceptionally unlikely; one where measurements show corruption is tolerably low; or traffic for applications that tolerate misdelivered or corrupted packets. Tunnels spanning networks that do not cooperate closely MUST still use the checksum.

Extra requirements include:

  • Using the checksum MUST be the default configuration.
  • The decapsulator SHOULD allow zero-checksum mode on only a single UDP destination port, and MUST check that the source and destination IPv6 addresses are valid for the tunnel, discarding the packet otherwise.
  • The encapsulator SHOULD use different IPv6 addresses for each zero-checksum tunnel.
  • Traffic MUST be actively monitored for errors by the operator, and measures SHOULD prevent it from escaping to the general Internet.

Middleboxes that validate or update UDP checksums, such as NATs and firewalls, will not pass IPv6 datagrams with a zero checksum. There is no fallback to a checksum when a path change sends a tunnel through such a device, so the tunnel is black-holed.
sections.plainLanguage: The check number on the envelope protects against smudged addresses. You may skip it only in well-run private networks that watch for problems and agree to the risk.

sections.title: Congestion Considerations
sections.content:
UDP tunnels share paths with other flows, so congestion control matters (RFC 5405, RFC 2914). IP traffic is generally assumed to be congestion controlled, so where MPLS-in-UDP carries IP traffic known to be congestion controlled, it MAY be used within one network or across cooperating networks.

MPLS also carries traffic that is not necessarily congestion controlled, such as pseudowire or VPN traffic with bandwidth guarantees. Inside a UDP tunnel the identity of individual MPLS flows is lost, so MPLS Traffic Engineering cannot guarantee bandwidth to specific flows. Therefore such traffic MUST only use MPLS-in-UDP within a single operator's carefully provisioned network, or among closely cooperating operators. MPLS-in-UDP MUST NOT be used over the general Internet or non-cooperating operators to carry traffic that is not congestion controlled.

Measures to keep it from escaping include link isolation, packet filters on the UDP destination ports, restrictions in tunnel setup tools, and a Managed Circuit Breaker.
sections.plainLanguage: If a pipe carries water that does not slow down when the pipe is full, the pipe needs an owner who makes sure it is never overfilled. That is why it stays in managed networks.

sections.title: Security and Port Allocation
sections.content:
MPLS-in-UDP faces the same security problems as MPLS-in-IP and MPLS-in-GRE. By itself it cannot ensure integrity or privacy, nor let the decapsulator authenticate the encapsulator, so it SHOULD be secured with IPsec or DTLS. IPsec would hide the UDP header from intermediate routers, which defeats the point of using UDP. With DTLS, the destination port MUST be 6636 and that port MUST NOT be used for other traffic. DTLS allows a single session per encapsulator/decapsulator pair and requires unicast addresses.

The decapsulator is not required to validate the IP source address, except for IPv6 in zero-checksum mode. Corruption of a VPN label could leak traffic across VPN boundaries, so where isolation matters UDP checksums SHOULD be used with IPv4 and IPv6, and zero-checksum mode SHOULD NOT be used with IPv6.

IANA allocated UDP port 6635 (MPLS-UDP) and port 6636 (MPLS-UDP-DTLS).
sections.plainLanguage: A plain envelope can be read or swapped, so for secret mail put it in a locked box first. That box needs its own mailbox number.
